_meta.description: Federal OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, P.L. 119-21) 'no tax on tips' (IRC §224) and 'no tax on overtime' (IRC §225) above-the-line deduction parameters, plus per-state conformity (does the state income tax also allow the federal deduction). Drives /tips-tax-calculator and /overtime-tax-calculator and the state-page conformity blocks. Figures are FIXED statutory amounts for tax years 2025–2028 (not inflation-indexed).
_meta.confidence: high — federal figures double-researched and adversarially verified (0 of 21 refute attempts succeeded)

common.note: These are deductions that reduce federal taxable income, not credits and not a withholding exemption. The dollar benefit ≈ the deduction amount × your marginal federal income-tax rate. Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) still apply to tips and overtime.

overtime.qualifies: Only the FLSA-required overtime PREMIUM — the extra 'half' paid above your regular rate (0.5× regular rate), NOT the full time-and-a-half. Overtime required only by state law, contract, or a collective-bargaining agreement (not by FLSA §7) does not qualify.

sources.claim: Cap $12,500 single / $25,000 joint; MAGI phase-out over $150,000/$300,000 at $100 per $1,000; only the FLSA premium qualifies; SSN + MFJ required; FICA still applies.
Above-the-line deduction available to itemizers and non-itemizers; effective tax years 2025–2028.

P.L. 119-21 section 70202 (new IRC section 225, 'Qualified overtime compensation'): only overtime pay required by section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act 'that is in excess of the regular rate' counts, which is the extra half in time-and-a-half.
IRS Notice 2025-69 — safe-harbor / reasonable methods to compute the 2025 deduction and phase-out.

tips.qualifies: Cash or charged tips (cash, check, card, or tokens exchangeable for cash) paid voluntarily by the customer, in an occupation that 'customarily and regularly' received tips — per the Treasury final-regs occupation list. The $25,000 cap is a single per-return limit (it is NOT doubled for joint filers). Self-employed claimants are limited to net business income and specified-service trades (SSTBs) are excluded.

sources.claim: Cap $25,000 per return (same single and joint); MAGI phase-out over $150,000/$300,000 at $100 per $1,000; above-the-line; SSN + MFJ required; FICA still applies; tax years 2025–2028.

P.L. 119-21 section 70201 (new IRC section 224): qualified tips are cash tips (including charged and shared tips) received in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024; they must be voluntary, not negotiated and set by the payor; tips in a specified service trade or business (section 199A(d)(2)) do not count; a self-employed person counts tips only up to the business's gross income above its other deductions.
Treasury/IRS final regulations listing the occupations that customarily and regularly receive tips.
Treasury detailed tipped-occupation list (published 2025-08-27).

senior.qualifies: Anyone who attains age 65 on or before the last day of the tax year (TY2025 forms: born before January 2, 1961) with a work-eligible SSN on the return. $6,000 per qualified individual ($12,000 for a joint return where both spouses qualify). Married taxpayers must file jointly — MFS gets $0. Unlike tips/overtime this is a BELOW-the-line §151 deduction: it does not reduce AGI, MAGI, provisional income, or Medicare IRMAA, and it did NOT change how Social Security benefits are taxed (IRC §86 is untouched). Only 'a joint return' gets the $150,000 threshold — single, HoH, and qualifying surviving spouse all use $75,000. Not indexed for inflation.

sources.claim: $6,000 for each qualified individual; 65 by year-end; 6% of MAGI over $75,000 ($150,000 joint) reduces the per-person $6,000; joint return required if married; SSN required; tax years 2025–2028.
Per eligible individual ($12,000 total for a married couple where both spouses qualify); available to itemizers and non-itemizers; in addition to the existing extra standard deduction for 65+.

Schedule 1-A Part V: 'born before January 2, 1961'; enter $75,000 ($150,000 if married filing jointly); multiply the MAGI above that by 6% and subtract it from $6,000 for each qualifying person; if married you must file jointly. Part VI carries the total to Form 1040 line 13b, below AGI (line 11b), so it does not reduce AGI. Arithmetic: 6% is $60 per $1,000, so each $6,000 reaches $0 at $175,000 of MAGI ($250,000 joint), because 75,000 + 6,000 / 0.06 = 175,000.
Social Security benefit taxation (IRC §86) was NOT changed by P.L. 119-21; the senior deduction is applied after taxable benefits are calculated.

salt.qualifies: State and local income taxes (OR general sales taxes in lieu of income taxes, taxpayer's election) plus state/local real property taxes and personal property taxes (IRC §164(a), unchanged by OBBBA). Itemizers only — the cap limits Schedule A line 5e; non-itemizers get nothing from this provision. Cap: $40,000 (2025) / $40,400 (2026) / $40,804 (2027), then 101%/yr through 2029 (2028–2029 exact values pending IRS guidance; computed under the 101% rule as $41,212 / $41,624, and the computed thresholds are flagged), MFS = half. Phase-down 2025–2029 only: cap reduced by 30% of MAGI over $500,000 (2025) / $505,000 (2026) / $510,050 (2027) (MFS = half), never below the $10,000 ($5,000 MFS) floor. 2030+: flat $10,000 ($5,000 MFS), no phase-down. MAGI here = AGI + §911/§931/§933 exclusions (= AGI for nearly all US-resident filers).

sources.claim: P.L. 119-21 section 70120: strikes the $10,000 ($5,000 married filing separately) cap and inserts 'the applicable limitation amount (half the applicable limitation amount in the case of a married individual filing a separate return)': $40,000 for 2025, $40,400 for 2026, then 101% of the prior year through 2029, and $10,000 after 2029. Through 2029 it is reduced by 30% of MAGI over $500,000 (2025), $505,000 (2026), then 101% a year (half for married filing separately), never below $10,000; MAGI is AGI plus section 911, 931 and 933 exclusions. Arithmetic from the 101% rule: $40,804 for 2027, then $41,212.04 and $41,624.16 for 2028 and 2029 before any IRS rounding.

IRC section 164(b)(6)-(7) as codified: the 2026 cap is $40,400 and the threshold $505,000; the cap is reduced by 30% of MAGI above the threshold but never below $10,000; married filing separately gets half the cap and half the threshold ($20,200 and $252,500 for 2026), so its floor is $5,000; MAGI is AGI plus section 911, 931 and 933 exclusions; $10,000 ($5,000 married filing separately) after 2029.

SALT torpedo, arithmetic from the 30% phase-down in section 164(b)(7)(B): inside the phase-down range each extra $1 of MAGI adds $1.30 of taxable income, so the marginal rate is 1.3 x 35% = 45.5% (48.1% in the 37% bracket); in 2025 the cap reaches the $10,000 floor at $600,000 of MAGI (500,000 + 30,000 / 0.30). Section 70120 changes section 164 only at (b)(6) and the new (b)(7) and adds no limit on state pass-through entity taxes.

IRS Notice 2020-75: state and local income taxes imposed on and paid by a partnership or S corporation are deductible by the entity, and such a payment 'is not taken into account in applying the SALT deduction limitation' to its owners, which is what state pass-through entity tax (PTET) elections rely on.
2025 standard deduction (OBBBA-set): $15,750 single/MFS, $31,500 MFJ, $23,625 HoH.
2026 standard deduction (Rev. Proc. 2025-32): $16,100 single/MFS, $32,200 MFJ, $24,150 HoH.
SALT is not deductible under the AMT — taxes from Schedule A are added back on Form 6251 line 2a, so taxpayers in AMT get less or no benefit from the higher cap.

carLoan.statute: IRC §163(h)(4) 'qualified passenger vehicle loan interest' (added by OBBBA §70203)
carLoan.qualifies: Interest — not principal — on a loan used to buy a qualifying vehicle, up to $10,000 per RETURN per year (not per vehicle; a joint return is capped at $10,000 total, and each married-filing-separately return gets its own $10,000). The vehicle must be NEW (original use begins with you — used cars and lease-end buyouts do not qualify), a car/minivan/van/SUV/pickup/motorcycle (not an ATV, trailer, camper, or RV) under 14,000 lbs GVWR, have its FINAL ASSEMBLY in the United States (checkable from the VIN plant code at the NHTSA decoder or the final-assembly point on the window sticker), and be for personal (not business) use. The loan must be incurred after 2024-12-31, secured by a first lien on the vehicle, not a lease, and not from a related party. The VIN must be reported on the return (Schedule 1-A, Part IV). BELOW the line but available to itemizers and non-itemizers alike — it reduces federal taxable income only, NOT AGI. Married-filing-separately is eligible (unlike the tips/overtime/senior deductions). Phase-out: min(interest, $10,000) is reduced by $200 for each $1,000 (or portion thereof) of MAGI over $100,000 ($200,000 for a joint return only), never below zero. MAGI = AGI + §911/§931/§933 exclusions (= AGI for nearly everyone). Tax years 2025–2028 only; not indexed for inflation.
eligibilityChecklist: New vehicle — original use commences with you (used cars and lease-end buyouts do not qualify)
Final assembly in the United States (VIN plant code or the window-sticker final-assembly point)
Loan incurred after 2024-12-31, secured by a first lien on the vehicle
Personal use, not business or commercial — and not a lease

sources.claim: IRC section 163(h)(4) as codified: up to $10,000 a year of qualified passenger vehicle loan interest, reduced by $200 for each $1,000 (or portion) of MAGI over $100,000 ($200,000 joint), applied after the $10,000 cap. The vehicle's original use must begin with the taxpayer (so used vehicles do not qualify), and it must be a car, minivan, van, sport utility vehicle, pickup truck or motorcycle under 14,000 pounds with final assembly in the United States. The loan must be taken out after 2024, secured by a first lien, for personal use, not lease financing and not from a related party, and the VIN must be on the return. Tax years 2025 to 2028; the statute has no inflation adjustment for these amounts.

Deduction for car loan interest 2025–2028; phases out for MAGI over $100,000 ($200,000 joint); vehicle must have final assembly in the United States and original use starting with the taxpayer; available to itemizers and non-itemizers.
Claimed on new Schedule 1-A (Part IV), flowing to Form 1040 line 13b after AGI — reduces taxable income, not AGI; VIN reported on the return.

Proposed regulations REG-113515-25 (Federal Register, January 2, 2026), proposed section 1.163-16: the $10,000 limit applies per federal return, so a joint return gets $10,000 in total and each married-filing-separately return gets its own $10,000; a lessee who buys the car at the end of the lease does not qualify, because original use began with the leasing company; lease financing is excluded; US final assembly can be shown from the VIN plant of manufacture (49 CFR 565) or the vehicle label (49 CFR 583.5(a)(3)).

charitable.statute: IRC §170(p) non-itemizer deduction (OBBBA §70424); IRC §170(b)(1)(I) 0.5%-of-contribution-base floor for itemizers (OBBBA §70425); IRC §68 itemized-deduction limitation, the '2/37 rule' (OBBBA §70111)
charitable.qualifies: Three OBBBA charitable changes, all effective for tax years beginning after 2025-12-31 and all PERMANENT (no 2028 sunset). (1) Non-itemizers: a §170(p) deduction of up to $1,000 (single/HoH/MFS/QSS) or $2,000 (MFJ) for CASH gifts to §170(b)(1)(A) public charities — NOT donor-advised funds, §509(a)(3) supporting orgs, or private non-operating foundations; non-cash gifts do NOT qualify; no carryforward. Claimed via §63(b)(4), i.e. subtracted AFTER AGI to reach taxable income — it lowers federal income tax but does NOT reduce AGI (so no IRMAA/ACA/SS-taxability effect), same structure as tips/overtime/car-loan. (2) Itemizers: only charitable contributions exceeding 0.5% of the contribution base (AGI) are deductible on Schedule A (§170(b)(1)(I)); the first 0.5% of AGI is lost. (3) 37%-bracket itemizers: §68 reduces TOTAL itemized deductions (all of them, not just charitable) by 2/37 of the lesser of (total itemized) or (taxable income over the 37% threshold), capping the benefit at 35 cents per dollar. The pre-existing 60%-of-AGI ceiling on cash gifts to public charities was made permanent.

sources.claim: IRC section 170(p) as amended: a non-itemizer may deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint) of cash gifts to section 170(b)(1)(A) organizations, not to section 509(a)(3) supporting organizations or donor advised funds, figured without the section 170(d)(1) carryover; section 170(b)(1)(I): itemized gifts count only above 0.5% of the contribution base.

IRC section 63(b) as codified: a non-itemizer's taxable income is AGI minus the standard deduction, personal exemptions under section 151, section 199A, and the deductions in sections 170(p), 224, 225 and 163(h)(4)(A), so section 170(p) is subtracted after AGI and does not reduce AGI.
IRC section 62(a) as codified: the above-the-line list has no reference to section 170 or 170(p), so the non-itemizer charitable deduction does not reduce AGI.

P.L. 119-21 section 70111 rewrites IRC section 68 from 2026: itemized deductions are reduced by 2/37 of the lesser of the itemized deductions or the taxable income (plus those deductions) above where the 37% bracket starts. Arithmetic: 2/37 is 5.4054%, so a filer in the 37% bracket saves 35 cents per dollar deducted. Section 68 has no carryover rule.
Enrolled statute of record: OBBBA §70424 (non-itemizer §170(p)), §70425 (0.5% floor §170(b)(1)(I)), §70111 (§68 limitation). Permanence and 2026 effective dates.

P.L. 119-21 section 70425, from 2026: itemized charitable gifts count only above 0.5% of the contribution base (generally AGI) (section 170(b)(1)(I)); amounts the floor disallows carry forward only from years in which a percentage-of-AGI ceiling is exceeded (section 170(d)(1)(C)); the 60% ceiling for cash gifts to public charities no longer has an end date. Arithmetic: on $500,000 of AGI the first $2,500 of gifts is disallowed; on $175,000 of AGI a $2,500 gift leaves $1,625 deductible (2,500 minus 875).

mip.statute: IRC §163(h)(3)(E) 'Mortgage insurance premiums treated as interest' — the termination clause (E)(iv) is permanently disabled by new §163(h)(3)(F)(i)(III), added by OBBBA §70108(a)(1)(D) ('Clause (iv) of subparagraph (E) shall not apply'). The deduction (E)(i)), the 10%-per-$1,000-or-fraction-thereof AGI phaseout (E)(ii), and the pre-2007-contract limitation (E)(iii) were never repealed and remain operative verbatim. 'Qualified mortgage insurance' is defined at §163(h)(5)(E) (VA, FHA, Rural Housing Service, and private MI). Prepaid/upfront premiums are governed by §163(h)(5)(F) + Treas. Reg. §1.163-11.

reporting.scheduleALine: 8d (2021-vintage — the last year the deduction was in effect; the 2026 Schedule A is not yet final, re-verify at form release)

mip.qualifies: Effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025 (OBBBA §70108(b)), permanent, not indexed for inflation. Premiums for monthly PMI (conventional loans), FHA annual MIP, FHA upfront UFMIP, VA funding fees, and USDA (Rural Housing Service) guarantee fees paid or accrued in connection with acquisition indebtedness on a qualified residence are treated as deductible home-mortgage interest on Schedule A — itemizers only, no non-itemizer alternative. The deductible amount is reduced (never below zero) by 10% for each $1,000 ($500 MFS) or fraction thereof that AGI exceeds $100,000 ($50,000 MFS) — fully eliminated once AGI exceeds $109,000 ($54,500 MFS); MFJ shares the single/HoH $100,000 threshold (no separate joint threshold, a marriage-penalty structure). Only mortgage insurance contracts issued after December 31, 2006 qualify. Lump-sum prepaid premiums (FHA UFMIP, single-premium/split-premium PMI) must be amortized ratably over the shorter of the loan's stated term or 84 months starting the month the insurance was obtained; the unamortized balance is lost (not deductible) if the mortgage is paid off or refinanced early. VA funding fees and USDA guarantee fees are exempt from amortization — fully deductible in the year paid, even as a lump sum. Reported via Form 1098 Box 5 (prepaid premiums included, $600-per-mortgage reporting threshold) flowing to Schedule A line 8d (2021-vintage line; the 2026 form is not yet final).

sources.claim: OBBBA §70108: amends §163(h)(3)(F) to strike the pre-2026 sunset and insert new subclause (III), 'Mortgage insurance premiums treated as interest.—Clause (iv) of subparagraph (E) shall not apply,' making the MIP deduction permanent and effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; (E)(ii)/(iii) untouched.

IRC section 163(h)(3)(E) as codified: the deduction (clause (i)); the phaseout, which cuts it by 10% for each $1,000 ($500 MFS) or fraction of AGI over $100,000 ($50,000 MFS) (clause (ii)); and the limit to contracts issued after 2006 (clause (iii)). Section 163(h)(3)(F)(i)(III), added by P.L. 119-21 for tax years after 2025, switches off the clause (iv) termination.

IRC section 163(h)(5)(E) (numbered (h)(4)(E) until P.L. 119-21 section 70203 inserted the car loan paragraph): 'qualified mortgage insurance' is VA, FHA or Rural Housing Service mortgage insurance plus private mortgage insurance under the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998; section 163(h)(3)(E)(iii) excludes contracts issued before January 1, 2007.

IRC section 163(h)(5)(F) and Treas. Reg. section 1.163-11: prepaid mortgage insurance premiums are spread evenly over the shorter of the mortgage's stated term or 84 months from the month the insurance was obtained; no deduction for the unamortized balance if the mortgage is paid off early; the rule does not apply to VA or Rural Housing Service mortgage insurance.
IRS Pub 936 Mortgage Insurance Premiums Deduction Worksheet: no deduction if AGI is more than $109,000 ($54,500 if married filing separately).

IRS Instructions for Form 1098 (Rev. December 2026): Box 5 'Mortgage Insurance Premiums' — enter total premiums of $600 or more paid for the tax year, including prepaid premiums, for qualified mortgage insurance.
2026 standard deduction (Rev. Proc. 2025-32): $16,100 single/MFS, $32,200 MFJ, $24,150 HoH — the itemize-vs-standard gate this deduction depends on (no benefit to non-itemizers).

qcd.statute: IRC §408(d)(8) 'Distributions for charitable purposes' (qualified charitable distributions). Annual limit inflation-indexed under §408(d)(8)(A) flush language + §1(f)(3) since 2024. NOT an OBBBA provision; permanent.

ageStandardDeductionAddition._source: IRC section 63(f) additional standard deduction for age 65 or older. It is a different deduction from the $6,000 senior deduction in federal.senior; do not count them twice. Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 4.14(3), https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf: for 2026 the amount is $1,650, increased to $2,050 if the individual is also unmarried and not a surviving spouse. Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.15(3), https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-24-40.pdf: $1,600 and $2,000 for 2025. So the higher amount goes to single and head of household filers only; a married person filing separately is still married, and a qualifying surviving spouse is a surviving spouse, so both get the base amount ($1,650 for 2026, $1,600 for 2025), the same as each spouse on a joint return.

qcd.qualifies: A QCD lets an IRA owner age 70½+ send up to $111,000 (2026; indexed, per person) directly from the IRA trustee to a §170(b)(1)(A) public charity. The amount is EXCLUDED from gross income (§408(d)(8)(A) 'shall not be includible in gross income') — it never enters AGI, and no separate charitable deduction is allowed (no double-dip). It counts toward that year's RMD (RMD age is 73 under SECURE 2.0, so QCDs are available ~2.5 years before RMDs begin). Must go DIRECTLY from the trustee to the charity — NOT a donor-advised fund, private foundation, or §509(a)(3) supporting organization — and the entire gift must otherwise be 100% deductible under §170 (no return benefit). From an IRA only (not a 401(k); not an ongoing SEP/SIMPLE). Not subject to federal withholding (deemed elected out under §3405(a)(2)). The excludable amount is reduced by post-70½ deducted IRA contributions.

sources.claim: 2026 annual QCD limit $108,000 → $111,000; one-time split-interest $54,000 → $55,000.

§408(d)(8): 'shall not be includible in gross income'; age 70½ 'attained'; direct-by-trustee to §170(b)(1)(A) org OTHER THAN a §509(a)(3) supporting org or §4966(d)(2) DAF; entire distribution must be allowable as a §170 deduction; $100,000/$50,000 base amounts indexed after 2023.

Pub 590-B QCD mechanics: 'at least age 70½ when the distribution is made'; 'made directly by the trustee of your IRA (other than an ongoing SEP or SIMPLE IRA)'; 'A QCD will count towards your required minimum distribution'; maximum annual exclusion $108,000 (2025) / $111,000 (subsequent-year worksheet); taxable-portion-first; post-70½ deductible-contribution offset; RMD 'Age 73 for tax years 2023 and later'.

IRS Notice 2007-7, Q&A-40: a qualified charitable distribution is not subject to withholding under section 3405, because the IRA owner who requests it is deemed to have elected out of withholding under section 3405(a)(2).

Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 4.14(3): for 2026 the section 63(f) additional standard deduction for the aged or blind is $1,650, increased to $2,050 if the individual is also unmarried and not a surviving spouse.

Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.15(3): for 2025 the section 63(f) additional standard deduction for the aged or blind is $1,600, increased to $2,000 if the individual is also unmarried and not a surviving spouse.
Form W-4R: for nonperiodic payments, including IRA distributions payable on demand, the default withholding rate is 10%, and the recipient can choose a different rate on line 2.

states._note: Per-state conformity filled from the state re-verification pass. conformity values: 'no_wage_income_tax' | 'decouples' (federal deduction does NOT reduce state tax) | 'conforms' (does reduce state tax) | 'partial'/year- or deduction-dependent (see per-field). Each carries tips/overtime × 2025 / 2026plus where they differ, plus a source.

north-dakota.name: North Dakota

senior.note: North Dakota starts from your federal taxable income and follows federal changes automatically, so the $6,000 federal senior deduction lowers your North Dakota tax too, for 2025 and 2026.
senior.sourceTitle: North Dakota 2025 individual income tax booklet
senior._sourceNote: 2025 booklet: 'The starting point for computing North Dakota taxable income perpetually conforms to the computation of federal taxable income. As a result, the federal changes to income and deductions that impact the computation of federal taxable income are by default included in the starting point for computing North Dakota taxable income for all years.' It then lists 'an additional $6,000 for some seniors'. N.D.C.C. 57-38-30.3(2): 'North Dakota taxable income' means the federal taxable income of an individual 'as computed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended' (https://ndlegis.gov/cencode/t57c38.pdf). Schedule ND-1SA has no add-back for it. No regular session in 2026; the January and September 2026 special sessions passed nothing touching chapter 57-38.

carLoan.note: North Dakota starts from your federal taxable income and follows federal changes automatically, so the federal car loan interest deduction lowers your North Dakota tax too, for 2025 and 2026.
carLoan.sourceTitle: North Dakota 2025 individual income tax booklet
carLoan._sourceNote: The 2025 booklet never mentions car loan interest; it backs only the general point that ND follows federal taxable income. The row rests on rolling conformity in N.D.C.C. 57-38-30.3(2): 'North Dakota taxable income' means 'the federal taxable income of an individual, estate, or trust as computed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended' (https://ndlegis.gov/cencode/t57c38.pdf; host unreachable from our network on 2026-10-02, text read from the 2026-07-08 Wayback copy). The IRC 163(h)(4) deduction is taken in computing federal taxable income, so it carries into ND taxable income unless ND adds it back, and it does not. Office of State Tax Commissioner, OBBBA impacts presentation to the interim committee (https://ndlegis.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/committees/69-2025/27.5038.02000presentation1300.pdf): 'e. Deduction for certain auto loan interest up to $10,000 2025-2028' with an estimated cost to North Dakota collections of $3 million in each of FY26 and FY27. Schedule ND-1SA has no add-back for it; the 2026 special sessions passed nothing touching chapter 57-38.

north-dakota.note: North Dakota is a rolling-conformity state that starts from federal taxable income, so it automatically incorporates the federal overtime and tips deductions for tax years 2025–2028. No decoupling legislation has been enacted.
north-dakota.sourceTitle: North Dakota Office of State Tax Commissioner: OBBBA impacts presentation, tips and overtime flow through to ND tax

district-of-columbia.name: District of Columbia

senior.note: DC does not allow the $6,000 federal senior deduction on your 2025 DC return. From 2026 it does, under the same DC laws as the tips and overtime rule: D.C. Act 26-416, in effect until November 11, 2026, and D.C. Act 26-418, expected to take effect around November 20, 2026. DC's tax office has not yet published 2026 forms that show this deduction.
senior._sourceNote: Quoted in this row's _sourceNote: 47-1803.04(d)(9) disallows the 151(d)(5)(C) senior deduction for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026, and (e)(6) allows it for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025 (Act PDF page 192). Open reading, flagged 2026-10-02: 47-1803.04(a)(1) allows an individual 'either the standard deduction or itemized deductions (including the additional deductions set forth in subsection (e) of this section, if applicable)', and (b) bars other additions to the standard deduction for a filer who takes it, except as the chapter provides. Read together they could limit the (e) deductions to itemizers. The (e) lead-in allows them 'in computing net income of any individual', and the fiscal impact statement treats them as open to all filers; the calculator follows that until OTR's 2026 forms settle it.

carLoan.note: DC does not allow the federal car loan interest deduction on your 2025 DC return. From 2026 it does. The rule is in D.C. Act 26-416, an emergency law in effect until November 11, 2026; the permanent law with the same rule, D.C. Act 26-418, is expected to take effect around November 20, 2026. DC's tax office has not yet published 2026 forms that show this deduction.
carLoan._sourceNote: D.C. Act 26-416 (B26-0724), sec. 7112(e), adds D.C. Code 47-1803.04. Page 191, subsection (d) 'Deductions not allowed': '(8) Personal car loan interest. Any deduction for personal car loan interest allowed under § 163(h)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026'. Page 192, subsection (e) 'Additional deductions allowed': '(5) Personal car loan interest. Any deduction for personal car loan interest allowed under § 163(h)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025'. D.C. Act 26-418 (B26-0661) carries the identical text (https://lims.dccouncil.gov/downloads/LIMS/61627/Signed_Act/B26-0661-Signed_Act.pdf?Id=244269). The row's _watch covers the emergency act's expiry. Open reading, flagged 2026-10-02: 47-1803.04(a)(1) allows an individual 'either the standard deduction or itemized deductions (including the additional deductions set forth in subsection (e) of this section, if applicable)', and (b) bars other additions to the standard deduction for a filer who takes it, except as the chapter provides. Read together they could limit the (e) deductions to itemizers. The (e) lead-in allows them 'in computing net income of any individual', and the fiscal impact statement treats them as open to all filers; the calculator follows that until OTR's 2026 forms settle it.

district-of-columbia.note: Under the DC law in effect now, you can take the federal tips and overtime deductions on your DC return starting with tax year 2026. For 2025 you cannot, so for that year they lower your federal tax only. The law in effect now is an emergency DC law (D.C. Act 26-416) that lasts until November 11, 2026. The District's 2027 budget law (D.C. Act 26-418) has the same rule; Congress is reviewing it, and it is expected to take effect around November 20, 2026. DC's tax office has not yet published 2026 forms that show these deductions.
district-of-columbia._sourceNote: Swapped 2026-10-02 off Kiplinger ('Emergency Tax Bill Ends... Tip, Overtime Tax Breaks in D.C.'), which described the December 2025 decoupling (D.C. Act 26-214, then temporary D.C. Law 26-89, effective 2026-02-12, disapproved by Congress in Pub. L. 119-78, expired 2026-09-25). That law disallowed IRC 224 and 225 with no year limit, so it was the basis for the old 2026 'no'. It is superseded. oregon.name: Oregon

senior.note: Oregon does not allow the $6,000 federal senior deduction on your Oregon return, in 2025 or 2026. Oregon's tax guide lists the federal deduction for people 65 and older among the federal rules Oregon does not follow, and Oregon's 2026 tax law, SB 1507, did not change that.
senior._sourceNote: Publication OR-17 (150-101-431, Rev. 01-29-26), page 7, 'Oregon exceptions to federal tax law: ... IRC Section 151 deduction for personal exemptions. This includes the deduction for taxpayers who are age 65 or older at the end of the year.' The senior deduction is IRC 151(d)(5)(C). Legislative Revenue Office, Report #2-25 (August 2025), page 2: 'An earlier version of H.R. 1 changed federal law in such a way as to cause Oregon to be automatically connected to the deduction. Ultimately, however, the enacted federal language does not result in an automatic connection.' (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/lro/Documents/HR%201%20Title%20VII%20Revenue%20Impact%20Estimates%20RR2_25.pdf). SB 1507 (2026 Laws ch. 142) contains no reference to IRC 151. Oregon's own extra standard deduction for age 65 ($1,200 per box for 2025, OR-17) is separate and unaffected. 2026 Oregon forms are not yet published.

carLoan.note: Oregon allows the federal car loan interest deduction on your 2025 Oregon return. From 2026 it does not: Oregon's 2026 tax law, SB 1507, adds the interest back, so it no longer lowers your Oregon tax.
carLoan._sourceNote: 2026 on: SB 1507 (2026 Laws ch. 142) sec. 2, added to ORS chapter 316: 'There shall be added to federal taxable income an amount equal to qualified passenger vehicle loan interest paid by the taxpayer and deducted on the taxpayer's federal income tax return in the tax year, as provided in section 163(h)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code.' Sec. 10(1): 'Sections 2 and 5 of this 2026 Act ... apply to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026.' 2025: Publication OR-17 (150-101-431, Rev. 01-29-26), page 70, 'Federal deduction for passenger vehicle interest paid (ORS 316.048) [Subtraction code 392] ... Oregon allows the same deduction for interest paid on a qualifying passenger vehicle loan that is allowed on your federal return' (https://www.oregon.gov/dor/forms/FormsPubs/publication-or-17_101-431_2025.pdf).

oregon.note: Oregon follows federal tax law as it changes, so the federal tips and overtime deductions also come off the income Oregon taxes. Oregon's 2026 tax law, SB 1507, does not add them back (it does add back the car loan interest deduction, from 2026).
oregon._sourceNote: Rewritten 2026-10-02 (the old note was 'Oregon conforms (rolling conformity); the deductions flow through to the state return'). ORS 316.048 makes federal taxable income the Oregon base, and ORS 316.012(2), as amended by SB 1507 sec. 38, ties the definition of taxable income to the Internal Revenue Code as it changes. 2025: Publication OR-17 (150-101-431, Rev. 01-29-26), page 70, 'Federal deduction for tip income (ORS 316.048) [Subtraction code 390] ... Oregon allows the same deduction for tip income that is allowed on your federal return' and 'Federal deduction for overtime wages (ORS 316.048) [Subtraction code 391] ... Oregon allows the same deduction for overtime wages that is allowed on your federal return' (https://www.oregon.gov/dor/forms/FormsPubs/publication-or-17_101-431_2025.pdf). 2026: SB 1507 (2026 Laws ch. 142) makes three additions to federal taxable income for the personal income tax: qualified passenger vehicle loan interest under 163(h)(4) (sec. 2), the 1202 small business stock exclusion (sec. 5) and 168(k) bonus depreciation (sec. 7). It adds nothing back for 224 tips or 225 overtime. Enrolled text: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/SB1507/Enrolled. checkedOn is this row's own last-checked date; /what-applies-to-me/ prints it in place of _meta.lastSourced.

alabama.name: Alabama
alabama.note: Alabama does not follow the full federal overtime deduction, but it has a smaller one of its own for tax years 2026 through 2028 (Act 2026-604). You can deduct the extra part of your overtime pay above your normal rate, the "half" in time and a half, up to $1,000 a year, on your Alabama return. You claim it when you file, so it does not change your paychecks. Because Alabama also lets you subtract your federal income tax, the federal overtime deduction raises your Alabama tax by about 5 cents per dollar it saves you, which can outweigh what this $1,000 deduction saves you. Tips get no Alabama deduction, and the federal tips deduction raises your Alabama tax the same way. Alabama's earlier, full overtime exemption ended June 30, 2025.
alabama._sourceNote: Re-verified 2026-10-02 against primary sources and swapped off the Governor's press release, which gave the $1,000 cap but neither the act number nor what counts. (1) The act: HB527 of the 2026 Regular Session is Act 2026-604 (ALISON record: status Enacted, viewEnacted https://arc-sos.state.al.us/cgi/actdetail.mbr/detail?page=act&year=2026&act=604). Its enrolled text adds Ala. Code 40-18-15(a)(29): 'For tax years beginning on and after January 1, 2026, and ending December 31, 2028, qualified overtime compensation received during the taxable year, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per taxpayer. For purposes of this deduction, qualified overtime compensation shall be defined and calculated pursuant to the provisions of 26 U.S.C. § 225.' Section 3 makes that section effective October 1, 2026. https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB527-enr.pdf (2) What counts: 26 U.S.C. 225(c)(1) limits qualified overtime compensation to overtime pay required by FLSA section 7 'that is in excess of the regular rate', the premium only. https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section225&num=0&edition=prelim (3) The Alabama Department of Revenue page cited in `source`: 'The deduction is the lesser of the actual overtime premium or a maximum annual amount of $1,000 per taxpayer', 'Only the premium portion of overtime wages is considered deductible overtime', and the W-2 box 12 code TT entry 'will not change wages, withholdings, or taxes on Form W2'. It names no income limit. (4) The earlier exemption: the Department's Act 2024-437 page, 'The Alabama income tax exemption applicable to overtime wages ends on June 30, 2025.' https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/individual-corporate/overtime-pay-exemption-amended/ Modeled in the paycheck engine (tax-data-2026.json alabama.tax.overtimePremiumDeduction) and priced at filing on /alabama-paycheck-calculator/.
